summary: Describes how to provide call transfer in SIP using extensions such as REFER and Replaces, covering blind, consultative and attended transfer. It is part of the SIP multiparty call control framework, and is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary: When a receptionist moves your call to a colleague, a transfer happens. This document explains the exact steps phones take to do it, whether the receptionist talks first or not.

subtitle: How SIP phones hand a call to someone else using REFER and Replaces, from blind to attended transfer.

tldr.problem: SIP users expect PBX-style call transfer, where one party hands another party's call to a third person, but SIP has no single transfer message.
tldr.mechanism: The Transferor sends a REFER that makes the Transferee send an INVITE to the Transfer Target, optionally with a Replaces header to take over a consultation call. The RFC walks through basic, consultative, attended and semi-attended flows.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice document that is part of the SIP multiparty call control framework. It prefers sending the REFER in a new dialog when that is safe, and covers failures, security and gateway issues.

today: RFC 5589 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 149) from June 2009, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 3515 and RFC 3891 rather than defining new SIP messages.

sections.title: Call Transfer in SIP
sections.content:
RFC 5589 describes call transfer capabilities and requirements in SIP (RFC 3261) as part of the multiparty call control framework. It uses the REFER method (RFC 3515) and the Replaces header field (RFC 3891) to deliver blind transfer, consultative transfer and attended transfer. The mechanisms are closely related to traditional, basic and consultation hold transfers.

A User Agent that fully supports the document supports REFER and Replaces on top of RFC 3261, uses a Contact URI that meets the requirements of Section 8.1.1.8 of RFC 3261, and supports the Target-Dialog header field (RFC 4538).

The RFC does not prescribe the flows exactly as shown. They illustrate best practice that reflects IETF consensus.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo explains how phones can pass a call along, the way a receptionist hands a call to a colleague, using a few special SIP messages.

sections.title: Actors and Roles
sections.content:
Every transfer has three actors:

  • Transferee: the party being transferred to the Transfer Target.
  • Transferor: the party who starts the transfer.
  • Transfer Target: the new party brought into a call with the Transferee.

For the multi-party scenarios the RFC adds four more roles. The Originator wants to call the Recipient. A Facilitator acts for the Originator and connects it to the Recipient through a Screener, who acts for the Recipient and decides whether to pass the caller on.
sections.plainLanguage: Three people matter: the one who moves the call (Transferor), the one whose call is moved (Transferee), and the new person they end up talking to (Transfer Target).

sections.title: Requirements
sections.content:
Six requirements drive the design:

  1. Any party in a SIP session must be able to transfer any other party at any point in that session.
  2. The Transferor and Transferee must not be removed from a session as part of the transfer transaction.
  3. The Transferor must know whether the transfer succeeded.
  4. The Transferee must be able to replace an existing dialog with a new dialog.
  5. The Transferor and Transferee should indicate support for the primitives needed for transfer.
  6. The Transferor should give the Transfer Target and Transferee information about the nature and progress of the transfer.

The RFC notes that requirement 2 does not force a different user experience from a PBX or Centrex, and that without it, behaviors such as ringback on transfer failure would be lost. Requirement 6 can be met by modeling the transfer as an ad hoc conference of three parties.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules say: anyone can pass a call along, nobody gets dropped by accident, and the person doing the passing finds out whether it worked.

sections.title: Using REFER and Choosing the Dialog
sections.content:
A REFER from the Transferor makes the Transferee send an INVITE to the Transfer Target. A successful REFER does not end the Transferor-Transferee session; if they want to end it, they must send a BYE. The media negotiated with the Transfer Target is independent of the earlier media, and the INVITE the Transferee sends has the same SDP body it would have had on its own.

The REFER can be sent in the existing INVITE dialog, which then carries both an invite usage and a subscription usage, or in a new dialog. The RFC's approach is to avoid dialog reuse because of the problems described in RFC 5057. Reuse was historically motivated by routing uncertainty, association with the invite usage, and authorization of out-of-dialog REFERs. GRUUs address the first, and the Target-Dialog header addresses the second.

The rule: if the Transferee supports target-dialog and the Transferor knows the Contact URI is routable outside the dialog, the REFER SHOULD be sent in a new dialog. If either is unknown, it SHOULD be sent inside the existing dialog. A Transferee MUST be prepared to receive a REFER inside or outside a dialog. A Transferor could validate a Contact URI by sending an OPTIONS request and getting a response.
sections.plainLanguage: You can pass a note to your friend in the conversation you already have, or send it separately. The memo says to send it separately when you are sure it will reach the right friend.

sections.title: Basic Transfer and Failures
sections.content:
In basic transfer the Transferor gives the Transfer Target's contact to the Transferee. The Transferee tries to reach the Target and reports the outcome to the Transferor through NOTIFY messages. The Transferor-Transferee relationship is kept (usually on hold), so the call is recoverable if the Target cannot be reached. The Target's contact is exposed to the Transferee and can be used for future calls. Participants SHOULD list REFER and NOTIFY in Allow headers and Target-Dialog in Supported.

If the Transferor does not intend to help with recovery, it can send a BYE as soon as the REFER transaction completes. This is known as unattended or blind transfer.

In the failure examples (target busy, target does not answer) the Transferor receives a failure report in a NOTIFY, takes the Transferee off hold and resumes the session.
sections.plainLanguage: You ask your friend to call the new person. You stay on the line until you hear it worked. If the new person is busy, you are still there to help.

sections.title: Consultation and Attended Transfer
sections.content:
Transfer with consultation hold means the Transferor first talks to the Transfer Target. A nice touch is for the consultation INVITE to tell the Target, for example in the display name, that the call relates to an intended transfer.

  • Exposing the Target: hold the Transferee, call the Target, hang up, then run a basic transfer. This resembles the PBX and Centrex experience.
  • Protecting the Target: hold the Transferee, call the Target, then reverse roles and transfer the Target to the Transferee. The Target's details stay hidden, but the Transferee is effectively called back, so it needs a way (such as Replaces) to match the new call.
  • Attended transfer: hold both, then send a REFER whose Refer-To carries an escaped Replaces header. The Transferee's INVITE replaces the consultation dialog.

Attended transfer SHOULD use the Target's Contact URI as the Refer-To URI unless it is suspected not to be routable outside the dialog; then the Address of Record is used and Require: replaces SHOULD be set. If the AOR fails, the Transferee may retry with the Contact URI.

Fallbacks cover a party without REFER support (a 501 Not Implemented, or perhaps a 405) and a Target without Replaces, which rejects the INVITE with 420 Bad Extension, after which the Transferor switches to basic transfer.

In semi-attended transfer the Transferor hangs up before the Target answers but the transfer continues as attended, with media played to the Target on answer so it does not hang up. The flows that use a CANCEL are NOT RECOMMENDED because of race conditions.
sections.plainLanguage: Before handing over the call, the receptionist first tells the new person 'I'm sending someone to you'. That is a consultation. In attended transfer the new person then takes over the line directly.

sections.title: Referred-By, Conferences, Multiple Parties and Gateways
sections.content:
Referred-By. The Transfer Target normally does not know who started a transfer. The Referred-By header (RFC 3892) lets the Transferor say so. The simple form copies the header into the triggered INVITE and is the least secure. A more secure form uses a signed Referred-By token passed in a message body.

Ad hoc conference. The Transferor can act as a conference focus (RFC 4579), and Transferee and Target subscribe to conference state (RFC 4575) to follow the transfer's progress. This meets requirement 6.

Multiple parties. One example chains an Originator, Facilitator, Screener and Recipient, and exposes the Recipient's contact. It only clarifies REFER semantics and should not be used as an implementation design.

Gateways. A gateway acts as a User Agent, so the flows apply to it too. Two gateway-specific issues are noted: coercing a call to hairpin through the same gateway, which may need future SIP extensions, and a glare-like race when a consultative transfer turns blind. The recommended behavior for that race is the approach of semi-attended transfer.
sections.plainLanguage: Extras include telling the new person who sent the call, setting up a three-way chat to keep everyone informed, and special cases when the call goes through a phone-network gateway.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Transfer is built on REFER and Replaces, so the security considerations of RFC 3515 and RFC 3891 MUST be followed. Any REFER MUST be appropriately authenticated and authorized, or calls may be hijacked. A UA may use local policy or human intervention to decide whether to accept it, and NOTIFY bodies should not leak private information.

An INVITE containing Replaces SHOULD only be accepted if it is authenticated and authorized. If the replaced dialog uses more media streams than the original, the user MUST authorize the added streams. Sections 7.1 and 7.2 address protecting the Target's Address of Record.
sections.plainLanguage: Only trusted callers should be allowed to move or take over a call, otherwise a stranger could steal it.
